clinicalPearls: Increased femoral anteversion is the commonest cause of in-toeing in children older than about three years and often becomes most obvious between three and six years of age
Affected children characteristically sit in the W position and run with an eggbeater or circumduction pattern, and the patellae point inward when standing
Clinically the hips show greater internal than external rotation, and the trochanteric prominence (Craig) test estimates the degree of anteversion with the child prone
Femoral anteversion is greatest at birth and decreases steadily through childhood, so persistent in-toeing usually reflects a lag in this normal derotation
The condition is generally physiological, frequently bilateral and symmetrical, and resolves spontaneously in most children by early adolescence
Reassurance and observation are the appropriate approach, as braces, shoe modifications, and exercises do not alter the natural history
A derotation femoral osteotomy is considered only for severe, persistent, cosmetically or functionally disabling deformity in an older child
reference.pathophysiology: Femoral anteversion is the forward angulation of the femoral neck relative to the transcondylar axis of the distal femur, which is high at birth and normally diminishes year on year through childhood as the femur remodels. When this physiological derotation lags, the residual excess anteversion internally rotates the lower limb, turning the patellae and feet inward to produce an in-toeing gait. It is regarded as a variation of normal skeletal maturation, reinforced by habitual sitting and sleeping postures such as W-sitting, rather than a structural disease, and pathological forms are largely confined to neuromuscular conditions such as cerebral palsy in which the derotation fails to occur.
additionalDifferentials: Internal tibial torsion as an alternative cause of in-toeing
Metatarsus adductus producing in-toeing at the foot
Neuromuscular in-toeing in cerebral palsy or spinal dysraphism
Developmental dysplasia of the hip affecting rotation
Legg-Calve-Perthes disease or slipped capital femoral epiphysis altering hip rotation
Compensatory rotation from a contralateral limb deformity
additionalInvestigations: Complete rotational profile including hip internal and external rotation measured prone
Trochanteric prominence (Craig) test to estimate anteversion clinically
Observation of the foot progression angle and gait pattern
Assessment of tibial torsion and foot alignment to localise the deformity
Hip radiographs where dysplasia, Perthes disease, or a slipped epiphysis is suspected
Computed tomography or three-dimensional rotational imaging reserved for preoperative planning
redFlags: Progressive or worsening deformity rather than the expected improvement with growth
Hip pain, limp, or restricted movement suggesting Perthes disease or a slipped epiphysis
Neurological signs indicating an underlying neuromuscular disorder
Short stature or dysmorphic features suggesting a skeletal dysplasia
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, with spontaneous resolution in the great majority of children as femoral anteversion decreases with growth, and there is no convincing evidence that ordinary physiological anteversion causes later osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Prescribing braces, twister cables, or special shoes that are ineffective and unnecessary
Failing to complete the rotational profile and missing a coexisting tibial or foot cause
Overlooking hip pathology such as a slipped epiphysis in the older or overweight child presenting with altered rotation
Recommending surgery before allowing time for physiological derotation
Attributing a neuromuscular gait disorder to simple anteversion
references: Staheli LT, rotational problems of the lower extremity
management: Reassure families that increased femoral anteversion is a physiological variant that resolves spontaneously with skeletal growth in the great majority of children
Observe with periodic clinical review of the rotational profile rather than active intervention
Avoid braces, shoe modifications, orthoses and corrective exercises, which do not alter the natural history
Discourage habitual W-sitting and encourage alternative sitting postures
Reserve femoral derotation osteotomy for the rare child with severe, persistent, functionally disabling deformity beyond the age of expected spontaneous correction
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics when in-toeing is unilateral, worsening, painful or associated with a neuromuscular condition such as cerebral palsy
